                MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS IN SUPPORT OF
                 NORTHERN INDIANA PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY LLC

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or

the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Northern Indiana Public Service Company

LLC (“NIPSCO”), a subsidiary of NiSource Inc., moves for leave to intervene in this proceeding

and submits these Comments in support of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc’s

(“MISO”) filing in the above-captioned docket to establish a Large Load Addition Resource Study

(“LARS”) process.2 MISO’s LARS Proposal is designed to be a permanent study process that

optimizes the MISO generator and load interconnection processes by providing expedited review

of the requested addition of 200 MW or greater loads together with new generation resources that

are electrically proximate to those loads. The LARS Proposal is just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory. Therefore, the Commission should approve MISO’s filing, effective December 2,

2026, as requested by MISO.

II.    MOTION TO INTERVENE
       A.      Description of NIPSCO

      NIPSCO is an Indiana limited liability company headquartered in Merrillville, Indiana, and

is a subsidiary of NiSource Inc. NIPSCO serves more than 877,800 natural gas customers and

492,700 electric customers across Northern Indiana. NIPSCO owns and operates approximately

3,880 megawatts of electric generating capacity and 2,981 miles of electric transmission lines.

NIPSCO is an electric load-serving entity and a transmission-owning member of MISO. NIPSCO

has transferred functional control of its transmission system to MISO, which serves as NIPSCO’s

Reliability Coordinator.

       B.      Grounds for Intervention

       NIPSCO is a transmission-owning member of MISO and owns and operates generation

facilities in the MISO footprint. NIPSCO also serves loads across Northern Indiana and expects to

serve the type of loads that are at issue in the LARS Proposal. NIPSCO therefore has a direct and



                                               2
 substantial interest in this proceeding that cannot be adequately represented by another party.

Pursuant to Rule 214, NIPSCO moves to intervene with full rights as a party in this proceeding.3

III.      BACKGROUND

          Recent projections of electricity demand growth and the Commission’s recent Show Cause

Order related to large load interconnections underscore the need for MISO to develop a process

for studying large loads and the generation intended to serve them.4 Specifically, MISO’s 2026

Reliability Imperative Report found that data centers, manufacturing expansion, and electrification

will drive annual load growth by 1% to 2% through 2044. To address long-term resource adequacy

issues, the fast connection of new resource additions is paramount for supporting large load growth

and ensuring reliability as reflected in MISO’s 2026 Planning Resource Auction Results.

          The Department of Energy’s (“DOE”) Speed to Power Initiative, likewise reflects the need

to accelerate the development of generation and transmission infrastructure to serve growing load.

In the Show Cause Order issued by the Commission on June 18, 2026, the Commission identified

potential gaps in the MISO Tariff concerning study procedures and services for the interconnection

of generation with electrically proximate large loads.5 The Commission directed MISO to provide

           For its part, NIPSCO, like many other electric utilities in MISO, is facing an unprecedented

level of interest from customers that desire to locate in NIPSCO’s electric service territory. While

historically, a new customer may inquire about adding a few MW of service and an inquiry for 10-

20 MW was considered a large load addition, new inquiries are now seeking to establish hundreds

or in some cases thousands of MW of new load. These new customers are also emphasizing the

desire for reliable and stable service to begin as soon as possible and the ability to interconnect

quickly. New generation in the MISO footprint is urgently needed in order to reliably

accommodate this growth, and accordingly new processes designed to expedite and integrate the

study process for the interconnection of large loads and their associated new generation are critical.

           The LARS Proposal addresses these resource adequacy concerns and the need to streamline

the MISO generator and load study process. Under the LARS Proposal, MISO would provide an

expedited pathway for studying qualifying large loads together with associated new generation

resources. While LARS Interconnection Customers will remain responsible for meeting the

requirements of MISO’s standard Generator Interconnection Queue, generation and load studies

will be conducted together under a single application.7 Also, Large Load Generator

Interconnection Agreements would be executed in 120 days.8 Leveraging the successes of MISO’s

existing Expedited Project Review process for new electric transmission projects (“EPS”), and

Expedited Resource Addition Study process for new generation facilities (“ERAS”), this LARS

 Proposal and its expedited timeframe is expected to integrate new large loads to the MISO region

in a timely and reliable manner.9 Unlike the ERAS process, which is a short-term fix to process

interconnection requests for generation necessary to meet significant, near-term needs, the LARS

Proposal is a permanent study process that would address MISO’s long-term need to interconnect

large loads and their associated generation.

           Importantly, the LARS Proposal contains several requirements that allow MISO to study

the new load impacts with greater certainty and reduce the risks of speculative generation or load.

These include the mandatory pre-submission coordination activities that require that the entities

involved in each LARS Application are aligned on all relevant details including the point of

interconnection and an agreement demonstrating the exact output the generating facility will use

to serve the associated load.10 In addition, the LARS Associated Transmission Customer, or Load

Serving Entity, must submit a non-refundable fee of $250,000 along with the LARS Application.

Forty-five days in advance of submitting the joint LARS application, the interconnection customer

must notify the transmission owner of its intentions to participate in LARS. After receiving the

request, the transmission owner must meet with the interconnection customer and any impacted

parties.11 These pre-submission coordination activities are designed to increase the efficiency of

MISO’s review by having all of the necessary details agreed upon prior to filing the LARS

Application.

           The LARS Process provides further certainty because LARS applications must also include

a signed agreement between the interconnection customer and owner or controller of the associated

new load for at least five years.12 This minimum service period provides assurance that the load

and generation will come online and all affected parties’ investments in the projects are warranted.

Finally, and importantly, the generation and proximate load must remain paired for a minimum of

fifteen years to ensure that resources are not reallocated to existing load and the LARS Process is

not misused.13

          MISO first introduced the LARS Proposal at the July 16, 2026 Large Load Working Group

meeting and revised the original proposal to address mismatches between the existing MISO study

processes and the LARS study processes in response to feedback from stakeholders.14

IV.       COMMENTS IN SUPPORT

          NIPSCO supports MISO’s LARS Proposal. By coordinating the study of qualifying large

loads and associated generation, the LARS Proposal offers a mechanism to identify necessary

network upgrades and bring new resources online while preserving reliability.15 It also addresses

the gaps in MISO’s Tariff as identified by the Commission in the Show Cause Order. MISO’s 2026

Reliability Imperative Report, the MISO’s 2026 Planning Resource Auction Results, and DOE’s

Speed to Power initiative all point to a high level of near-term reliability and resource adequacy

risk brought about by large load additions.16 While MISO has made recent strides in addressing

issues with its interconnection initiatives such as the existing EPR and ERAS processes, LARS

presents a permanent solution to NIPSCO’s and other MISO participants’ imminent needs to bring

Proposal provides a cost-effective tool to address the intersection of large load and generation, as

well as identify more optimized Network Upgrades at an expedited rate.17

          A.     The LARS Proposal is Necessary to Address MISO’s Short-Term Needs

          MISO’s existing interconnection process as set forth in Attachment X of MISO’s Tariff (the

Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”) process) alone is insufficient to bridge the corresponding needs

of new generation and large expected load growth throughout the MISO footprint. While the DPP

process is well-suited to address NIPSCO’s interconnection needs for normal load growth, the

scale and timing of large load interconnections present a different challenge. NIPSCO and other

MISO Market Participants are working with potential large load customers, such as data centers,

that have unprecedented service needs on short timeframes. NIPSCO, for example, is considering

requests to add between 3,000-8,000 MW primarily to serve megaload customers.18 The DPP

process was simply not designed to process the needs for both the interconnection of new large

load additions and the interconnection of new generation to supply energy to those loads in an

organized, coordinated and comprehensive fashion.

          Large loads present operational and reliability challenges and therefore require detailed

studies that enable affected parties to plan for reliability challenges. The LARS Proposal would

allow MISO to evaluate the associated load and generation using aligned assumptions and to

identify the upgrades required to accommodate both, through a single process. This coordinated

           B.     The LARS Proposal is a Just and Reasonable Solution

           As MISO outlines in its filing, the LARS Proposal is tailored to meet a specific need

identified by the Commission.19         It is self-limiting in that it is designed solely to study

generation/load pairs and maintains several guardrails in order to protect the DPP process and DPP

interconnection customers. MISO developed the LARS Proposal to ensure that the process works

in tandem with the DPP process and existing interconnection customers are not adversely

impacted. For instance, the LARS Proposal is designed to keep the transmission capacity available

for LARS applications separate from the transmission capacity headroom available throughout the

DPP cycle.20

           Further, LARS Applicants must commit to a substantially higher financial commitment

including a non-refundable $250,000 application fee. This payment will be used to fund the

additional tools, staffing, and process enhancement MISO needs to support its existing process and

LARS.21

           Finally, LARS applications cannot be modified after submission and prior to the execution

of the Large Load Generator Interconnection Agreement, ensuring that LARS Applicants avoid

sudden changes causing delays and withdrawals.22 The LARS Proposal is a just and reasonable

solution to MISO’s current resource adequacy dilemma.

 V.     CONCLUSION

       WHEREFORE, and for good cause shown, NIPSCO respectfully requests that the

Commission grant this Motion to Intervene and consider these Comments in support and accept

MISO’s LARS Proposal, effective December 2, 2026, as requested.
